newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian woman goes on trial for child torture.
newsitem.headline: Austrian woman goes on trial for child torture.

text.p: A woman accused of torturing her adopted mentally handicapped daughter and locking her in a coffin-shaped box at night for about 10 years went on trial in Vienna on Wednesday.
The woman, named only as Ernestine K, 65, is charged with instigating the abuse over that period of her daughter Maria, now 22, who is 50 to 60 percent mentally disabled.
Her husband, Walter, 67, is also charged with abuse and incarceration, while family friend, Irmengard M, is accused of being an accomplice.
Ernestine, a former religious education teacher, arrived at court wearing sunglasses and flew into a rage as she and her husband were surrounded by photographers.
A key piece of evidence, a wooden box measuring 160 cm by 55 cm and 33 cm deep, (64 inches by 22 and 13.2 deep) with 14 holes for air and a bolt on the outside, stood in a corner of the courtroom.

Prosecutor Michael Klackl alleged Ernestine K. began beating Maria in 1984 and frequently locked her in a garden shed with her hands tied together and her mouth sealed with sticking plaster when the couple went out.
"Ernestine robbed Maria of her childhood, youth and self-confidence, and her accomplices went along with it," Klackl said.

After Ernestine had the box built in December, 1995, Maria spent her nights locked inside until June 1996 when an anonymous call alerted the authorities to her ordeal and she was taken away from her parents' home in a Vienna suburb, he said.
Maria, who is undergoing psychiatric treatment, will not appear in court for the proceedings. Her testimony will be played in court on a video screen.
Ernestine denied all the charges except that of locking Maria in the box, saying she had hoped it would make her undersized daughter grow.
"You won't believe it but she grew 14 cm (5.5 inches)," said Ernestine, who has in the past had six adopted children besides Maria.
The box was intended as a "health bed" and Maria would always insist on being measured when she came out, she said.
"I never found her looking sad when I came to get her out. Sometimes she would say: 'Just a bit longer, Mummy!'"
The wooden box was found smeared with excrement and urine and contained blood-stained newspapers inside.
Klackl alleged Maria tried repeatedly to break out of the box, banging the roof and scratching the wooden boards. Her father and Irmengard admitted they had not dared to free her.
Ernestine said she had only meant the best for her daughter. "When I think about it now I wonder why I went to so much trouble," she said.
If convicted, Ernestine and her husband could face up to 10 years in jail.
